attack: The Co–Mo synergy is likely confounded by uncontrolled correlations with carbon, chromium, and vanadium. High-Co, high-Mo steels in published data are predominantly secondary-hardening or maraging alloys with elevated C and transition metals. When these are held constant, Co and Mo contributions become marginal. The hypothesis extracts a correlation but not a causal effect.

refuting_test.name: Low-carbon Co–Mo ablation study
refuting_test.description: From the pool, select steels with C ≤ 0.1 wt%. Partition into (1) Co ≥ 8, Mo ≥ 3 and (2) Co ≤ 1, Mo ≤ 1, ensuring Cr, V, Ni distributions are statistically matched between groups. Measure mean yield strength and perform a t-test. If group (1) exceeds group (2) by fewer than 150 MPa or p > 0.05, refute the hypothesis.

attack: The Ni₃Ti phase is assumed to precipitate and dominate strengthening without verification of thermodynamic stability at the tempering temperature. Competing phases—Ni-rich retained austenite, martensite decomposition products, or other intermetallics—are not ruled out. The hypothesis neglects temperature-dependent coarsening kinetics and the possibility that high Ni alone (without Ti) provides equivalent strength through matrix hardness.

refuting_test.name: Age-temperature-dependent Ni₃Ti precipitation kinetics
refuting_test.description: Quench steels with Ni ≥ 15, Ti ≥ 0.8 wt%, then conduct isochronal aging at 350 °C (below Ni₃Ti coarsening peak) and 550 °C (secondary-hardening window) for 1 h and 4 h respectively. Measure yield strength and perform TEM to confirm Ni₃Ti presence. If the 350 °C sample shows ≤100 MPa less strength than the 550 °C sample (indicating Ti precipitation is not rate-limiting), or if TEM finds no Ni₃Ti, refute the hypothesis.

attack: The mechanism conflates four independent variables (C, Cr, Mo, V) into one composite claim. Carbon alone drives martensite hardness; Cr and Mo are traded in industrial steels; vanadium at high levels (≥0.3 wt%) promotes delta-ferrite during solidification, which is embrittling. The region constraints are over-parameterized and may not represent a unique strengthening mechanism.

refuting_test.name: Orthogonal Mo–V substitution at fixed C–Cr
refuting_test.description: Hold C = 0.30 ± 0.05 and Cr = 4.5 ± 0.5 wt% constant. Prepare three experimental lots: (i) Mo = 1.5, V = 0; (ii) Mo = 0.5, V = 0.5; (iii) Mo = 0.5, V = 1.5. Quench and temper to a common hardness target (48 ± 1 HRC). If yield strength varies by <50 MPa across the three lots, the Mo–V combination is not a discrete strengthening mechanism and the hypothesis is refuted.

attack: The baseline assumes unspecified heat treatment (annealed or as-received). Low-carbon steels can exceed 600 MPa yield through controlled rolling, cold deformation, or even modest tempering. If the pool includes any work-hardened or cold-rolled samples without explicit annealing, the mean will violate the ≤600 MPa kill condition. Processing state is conflated with composition.

refuting_test.name: Heat-treatment stratified low-alloy baseline
refuting_test.description: From the pool, select steels with C ≤ 0.05, Co ≤ 0.5, Mo ≤ 0.5, Ti ≤ 0.1. Stratify by documented final heat treatment: (A) annealed/stress-relieved and (B) quench-tempered (35–40 HRC). Report mean yield for each stratum separately. If stratum (A) exceeds 600 MPa, or if prior deformation history is uncontrolled (e.g., 'as-received' includes cold-rolled material), the kill condition is violated.

attack: B₂ NiAl is assumed dominant, but at Al = 1–2 and Ni = 8–12 wt%, competing phases (Ni₃Al, Ni₃Nb, retained austenite) are thermodynamically feasible. The control group (Al ≤ 0.2, Ni ≥ 8) is not matched for Cr, Mo, V contents, confounding the Al effect with other strengtheners. High Ni suppresses the martensitic transformation, reducing martensite fraction and potentially lowering yield despite precipitate hardening.

refuting_test.name: CALPHAD equilibrium phase prediction + age-hardness kinetics
refuting_test.description: Use a multicomponent steel thermodynamic database (TCFE, MatCalc) to map phase fractions for the hypothesis region (Al ≥ 1, Ni ≥ 8, C ≤ 0.05) and a matched control (Al ≤ 0.2, Ni = 10 ± 1, same Cr/Mo/V range). If CALPHAD predicts B₂ comprises <30 vol% of precipitates or is thermodynamically unstable, refute the mechanism. Experimentally, conduct age-hardness curves; if hardness exhibits multiple peaks or broad kinetics inconsistent with a single precipitate phase, refute the hypothesis.
